title: Peltola Campaign Sues Alaska Over Rejected Ballots as Senate Race Remains on a Razor's Edge
snippet: Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign has filed a lawsuit against Alaska election officials to access rejected absentee ballot records while her high-stakes Senate battle against GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan hangs in the balance.
content:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — In a high-stakes legal battle amidst a razor-thin election, Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign has filed a lawsuit against the state of Alaska to gain access to records regarding rejected absentee ballots.

The court filing targets the Alaska Division of Elections after officials reportedly denied multiple requests from the campaign for data on disqualified votes. Peltola currently holds a slim lead of just over 600 votes over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, with roughly 30 percent of the total vote still uncounted.

Campaign Demands Immediate Transparency

In the legal filing, Peltola’s team argued that withholding the information prevents them from ensuring all eligible citizens have their voices heard in the uncalled race.

"Plaintiff cannot ensure that its voters’ lawful votes were properly counted without knowing whose absentee ballots were rejected or questioned, and why," the complaint reads. "Each hour and each day that Defendants deny Plaintiff the requested records to which it is entitled costs Plaintiff the opportunity to help ensure that qualified voters have their ballots counted."

State election officials quickly pushed back on Friday, arguing that publicizing the data before voters themselves are formally notified is neither required by law nor logistically sound.

"Alaska’s constitution and laws do not require the Division to provide this information in the manner requested by the campaign," the Division of Elections said in a statement. "Releasing preliminary information in the manner sought by the lawsuit would create additional burdens during ballot processing and could delay the timely counting of votes."

A Prolonged Vote Count and Ranked-Choice Runoff

The legal clash unfolds against the backdrop of Alaska's extended vote-counting timeline. Overseas and military ballots postmarked by Election Day are accepted up to 15 days after the election. While incremental updates may be released sooner, mandatory official reporting deadlines extend to Nov. 10, with final tabulations due by Nov. 18.

Because neither Peltola nor Sullivan has surpassed the 50 percent threshold, the contest is poised to trigger Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system. If an instant runoff is required, last-place candidates will be eliminated and their supporters' lower-choice preferences redistributed until one candidate captures a clear majority.

A victory for Peltola would represent an eighth Senate seat flip for Democrats nationwide. Meanwhile, Alaska election officials continue to process outstanding ballots under intense national scrutiny.
